1.pericope_label: I am jealous over you with godly jealousy; I have espoused you to one husband
debates: Whether the second clause of the first verse is a command or a statement: Chrysostom reads it as an affirmation that they do indeed bear with him and finds the shift a mark of confidence in their affection, and Ellicott agrees, tracing a movement from indignation to the softening memory of their loyalty; Calvin knows Chrysostom’s reading, grants that the Greek is ambiguous and either sense suits, and nevertheless follows the older Latin interpreter in taking it as a command, while Robertson notes only that the two forms are identical

What part the apostle claims in the marriage figure: Clarke takes him for the groomsman, comparing the Hebrew paranymphs and the Spartan magistrates who had charge of maidens, and Gill and Calvin likewise make all ministers friends of the bridegroom as the Baptist called himself, while Ellicott denies this and holds the verb properly describes the act of the father who gives his daughter in marriage

What the jealousy of God means: Barnes takes the phrase as a Hebraic superlative, the divine name marking whatever is signally great, so that a vehement attachment is meant, while Calvin distinguishes a jealousy springing from self-love from one cherished on God’s account and makes this the second, and Ellicott paraphrases it as a jealous care after the pattern of God’s own
outliers: Ellicott's reconstruction of the opponents' words from the two catch-words of the section, bearing with and folly, one occurring five times and the other eight, from which he infers that Titus had reported them saying something like, we can bear with him no longer, his folly is becoming altogether intolerable
Clarke's objection to supplying the name of God where the Greek has none, on the ground that too frequent use of the sacred name breeds a familiarity not conducive to reverence and godly fear
Clarke's derivation of the serpent's subtlety from doing all work, a versatility that accommodates itself to the caprices, prejudices and evil propensities of those it deals with
Wesley's inference from the temptation of Eve, who was simple and ignorant of evil, that we might be tempted even if there were no sin in us
Henry's remark that it is as much against the grain for a humble man to speak in his own praise as for a proud man to acknowledge his infirmities
Chrysostom's argument that a man who remembers sins God has forgotten, and calls himself unworthy of the very name of apostle, is plainly not speaking for the sake of glory

4.pericope_label: I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles
debates: Who the very chiefest apostles are: Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke and Calvin all take them for the true apostles, Henry holding the office equal in all of them and Calvin that God honoured this apostleship with marks of favour no less distinguished than those of John or Peter, while Ellicott denies this with some heat, calls it the insanity of controversy to suppose the words bear on the primacy of Peter, and renders the compound as an ironical coinage for the false teachers, in which Robertson follows him

Whether the closing clause of the fourth verse is serious or ironical: Barnes sets out three constructions and prefers the serious one, that if a better Saviour could be preached there would be propriety in receiving him, and Clarke, Wesley and Calvin take it the same way, Wesley adding that the case is impossible, while Robertson hears irony; Barnes alone records the third proposal, that the last word should be me rather than him

How the confession of rude speech consists with the gift of tongues: Barnes answers that the Spirit’s endowment enabled the apostles to speak languages they had never learned and did not perfect them in one learned in childhood, Clarke that the Spirit in general left them to their own language and prevented only equivocal expression, and Calvin that the substance of doctrine is one thing and the ornament of expression another
outliers: Ellicott's reconstruction of the Judaising taunt, that a man cutting and stitching all day could hardly be a doctor of the law, with his citation of the son of Sirach excluding the ploughman and the carpenter and the potter from the higher life of wisdom, since they shall not be found where parables are spoken

Clarke's aside that no tongue is so apt to seduce the understanding by its sounds and harmony as Greek, and that scholars in his own day fall into raptures over the music of a verse whose sense is little regarded and perhaps little worth
Henry's report of the guesses about the apostle's person, that he was of very low stature with a voice to match, or had some impediment of speech, perhaps a stammering tongue
Calvin's application to his own century, that men submit without difficulty to a harsh tyranny from their pretended bishops while not hesitating to treat Christ himself with contempt
Ellicott's conjecture that the different spirit points to a counterfeit inspiration like that of those who had interrupted the praises of the church with the cry of anathema against Jesus

7.pericope_label: I robbed other churches, taking wages of them, to do you service
debates: Where the word for being burdensome comes from: Barnes reports on Jerome’s authority that it is a provincialism of Cilicia, Ellicott traces it through the one Greek physician in whom it occurs and marks Jerome’s statement unproven for want of evidence, and Robertson counters that its use by that physician suggests a medical term in popular currency rather than a local dialect word

In what sense the other churches were robbed: Barnes and Ellicott ground it in the absence of an equivalent, a conqueror giving nothing for what he takes and wages being drawn from one employer while another is served, Gill grounds it in the disparity that the givers were poor and the served rich, and Calvin holds that what was contributed gratuitously was nonetheless due by the right of spiritual warfare

What the exaltation of the Corinthians was: Wesley makes it their becoming children of God, Clarke their receiving the pure doctrines of the gospel and being raised to the highest pitch of light and blessedness, and Calvin their becoming great through an abasement the apostle undertook of his own accord
outliers: Ellicott's derivation of the word for burdensome from the name of a fish of the torpedo kind, which benumbs whatever it touches, the same root giving us narcotic, with the gloss that the apostle did not benumb the Corinthians by demanding money of them

Ellicott's statement of the two-fold charge, that he was not above taking money from other churches but was too proud to take it from theirs, so that to take money at all was mean and not to take it from them was contemptuous

Calvin's defence of oaths, that two occur within three verses and both are lawful and holy because a good design and a legitimate reason are involved, so that to condemn all oaths indiscriminately is to act the part of fanatics who make no distinction between white and black

Wesley's question whether the poor have in all ages been more generous than the rich, drawn from the apostle's choosing help from the poor Macedonians rather than the rich Corinthians, with Calvin's exclamation at how few such givers were to be found in his own century

Ellicott's note that the word for region is peculiar to this apostle in the New Testament and is the source of our word climate, having begun as a term of science and passed into colloquial use, the province being named rather than the city so as to take in the port as well

12.pericope_label: False apostles, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ
debates: Whether the rival teachers really preached without pay: Calvin says they took no pay at all and made a show of uncommon zeal to allure the ignorant, and Ellicott defends the same inference against the objection that there is no evidence for it, holding that where it follows naturally from the language and nothing contradicts it that is evidence enough; against them Chrysostom says flatly that even this was a falsehood and they took money secretly, Clarke that the passage certainly does not mean they took nothing, Barnes that they probably contrived an ample support under various pretences, and Wesley that the boast was vain in them though not in the apostle

What the transforming of Satan refers to: Clarke ties it to the temptation in Eden and lists three forms in which the tempter comes, the subtle serpent, the roaring lion and the angel of light, and Barnes looks to the same scene and to the temptation in the wilderness, while Ellicott denies that any single incident is in view since the tense makes it a thing continually done, and looks instead to a claim of angelic authority made by the teachers at Corinth

What the ministers of righteousness were claiming: Ellicott reconstructs it historically, that they preached a righteousness they said the apostle neglected and claimed the authority of the one called the Just, presenting themselves as a revival of the ancient righteous ones, while Barnes takes it more simply of men of the blackest character putting on the appearance of the greatest sanctity
outliers: Chrysostom's opening challenge, that men who preach Christ and take no money and bring in no different gospel should be called false apostles, answered by saying that for this very reason most of all, since they make a pretence of these things in order to deceive, and that they do work indeed but pull up what has been planted

Cyril of Jerusalem's account of why the devil takes the shape of an angel, not that he may reascend where he was, for having made his heart hard as an anvil he has a will that cannot repent, but that he may envelop those living an angelic life in a mist of blindness

Calvin's simile that the pretence is exactly as if a harlot were to borrow the apparel of a decent matron, with his application to the golden titles of his own century, which he says are the golden cup in which Babylon gives poison to drink
Clarke's charge that under the third of the tempter's forms the persecutions and the fires and the horrors of the inquisition were all carried on in the name of religion
Robertson's gloss on the masquerade as gentlemen of the cloth and nothing but cloth, with his note that the apostle appears to have coined the word for false apostle
Ellicott's compositional note that the abruptness with which the next verse opens marks another pause in the dictation of the letter

16.pericope_label: Ye suffer fools gladly, seeing ye yourselves are wise
debates: What speaking not after the Lord means: Barnes sets out two senses, not by inspiration and not in imitation of the Lord’s example, prefers the second, and reports a third proposal that the words are not meant seriously; Robertson and Clarke take the second, Robertson noting that the meekness and gentleness of Christ had been appealed to a chapter earlier; Wesley takes the first in a qualified form, not by an express command though still under the direction of the Spirit; and Ellicott meets the question of inspiration directly and states the dilemma it raises

How the third clause of the twentieth verse should be rendered: Ellicott holds the supplied words wrong, since they turn the clause into a feeble repetition of the one before, and renders it of a man taking them in by guile, while Gill, Clarke and Wesley all take it of goods taken away, Clarke of exacted contributions and Wesley of open violence

Whom the reproach is aimed at: Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley all read the irony as addressed to the church at large for tolerating the impostors, while Calvin infers that it is not addressed to all indiscriminately but reproves particular persons who had behaved unkindly, and on the list of outrages sets out three constructions, preferring the charge of indolence but yielding to the reading commonly received on patristic authority
outliers: Ellicott's suggestion that the word rendered fool means rather insane than merely foolish, so that the plea is for the hearing most men would give even to one thought out of his mind

Ellicott's statement of the dilemma raised by the disclaimer, whether what is placed on the lower side of the line is to be counted inspired or uninspired, and whether admitting a human element here does not admit it elsewhere in Scripture as well

Barnes's report of the judgment that this is perhaps the most sarcastic sentence ever penned by the apostle, with Clarke's observation that it would be dishonourable in wise men to fall out with a fool and Wesley's that the irony is a beautiful one
Barnes's generalisation that a false religion always makes slaves and that only true Christianity leaves perfect freedom
Ellicott's tracing of the five clauses to the vices denounced in the woes against the Pharisees, with his note that the apostle was himself soon to be smitten on the face before a Jewish court
Robertson's remark that the apostle is plainly embarrassed at having to boast, whereas some men can do it with complete composure

21.pericope_label: Are they Hebrews? so am I. Are they ministers of Christ? I am more
debates: Whose reproach is spoken of: Barnes takes it of the apostle’s own, the things they counted disgraceful in him, and reports two further proposals, that the disgrace is the Corinthians’ or the false teachers’; Ellicott agrees that it is self-disparagement and hears behind it the taunt at his bodily infirmities; Clarke passes on a paraphrase making it the reproach cast on the Corinthians as profane and uncircumcised; and Gill leaves the possibilities open

What the name Hebrew signifies: Gill rejects at length the derivation from Abraham as betraying ignorance of the language, since Abraham himself bears the name, Calvin derives it from Heber on the evidence of Genesis, and Barnes from the verb meaning to pass over, applied to Abraham as one come from a foreign land, while Clarke and Ellicott are less concerned with the etymology than with what the three titles claimed

How many imprisonments lie behind the claim: Robertson reports that an early Roman writer numbered them at seven, that only five are known and only one before this letter, and asks whether there was one at Ephesus; Ellicott makes the same count and infers that the historian tends to understate rather than exaggerate these sufferings; Clarke observes that no instance appears of a false apostle imprisoned at all
outliers: Chrysostom's catalogue of the successive disclaimers, with his conclusion that if after doing all we ought still to call ourselves unprofitable, no forgiveness can be due to a man who exalts himself when nothing presses him, and his image of the Pharisee who suffered shipwreck even in harbour by striking on that rock

Ellicott's report of the insinuation behind the second name, that the apostle might be no more than the grandson of a proselyte, on whom a stigma rested which a proverb said was not effaced till the twenty-fourth generation, and his note that the calumny survived into a later sect which asserted he was a Gentile by birth
Ellicott's note that the stricter sort mourned the Greek version of the Scriptures on an annual fast-day as a national degradation

Calvin's marking of the turn, that having scattered their carnal glories like smoke by a breath of wind and having been content to stand level with them, he now separates himself from their society altogether when he has occasion to glory in good earnest
Clarke's thrust that had he preached the necessity of circumcision he would have been as free from opposition as they were
Ellicott's and Robertson's judgment that the word for folly is here sharpened to mean speaking deliriously, and is the very term of insult that had been flung at him

24.pericope_label: In perils oft, and beside all, the care of all the churches
debates: What the night and day in the deep refers to: Clarke reports the common supposition of an unrecorded shipwreck in which he saved himself on a plank, and also a theory that the word means a dreadful dungeon in a city of the Propontis, which he thinks unlikely; Ellicott takes the natural sense of one of the shipwrecks just named and reports the same dungeon theory, comparing the pit into which Jeremiah was let down; Wesley says only that he was probably floating on part of the vessel

Whether the fastings were chosen: Ellicott holds that, set apart from the hunger and thirst just named, they can hardly mean anything but times of self-chosen abstinence, and Calvin says the same, while Barnes leaves it open as either voluntary or involuntary

What the things that are without means: Barnes canvasses four proposals, that troubles from other sources are meant, or matters outside the regular routine of the office, or foreign affairs, or simply other things not to be mentioned, and prefers the last, while Clarke takes it of the outward things just enumerated and Wesley of what he suffered on account of others
outliers: The argument Barnes sets out at length, that the particulars here cannot be extracted from the history and yet nothing in them is contradicted by it, so that letter and narrative were written independently; with the observation that the mention of stoning comes nearer to a contradiction without incurring one than any case that writer had met with, since the history records one actual stoning and an earlier assault that was prevented

Gill's correction of the sentimental reading of the thirty-nine stripes, that the number was not abated out of tenderness nor because the offence was judged light, but reached the utmost rigour of the law as their tradition interpreted it

Ellicott's catalogue of what the daily rush consisted in, the visits of inquirers, the confessions of sin-burdened souls, the craving of perplexed consciences for guidance, the referring of household and church quarrels to his arbitration, and the arrival of messengers from distant churches

Clarke's citation of a nobleman's reflection on the hardship of it for a man of liberal education, wandering like a vagabond, hungry and almost naked, yet coming into the presence of persons of high life

Calvin's pastoral qualification, that such trials are not indispensably requisite in all, but that where they appear a greater and more illustrious testimony is afforded, and that the man so distinguished will not despise those less thoroughly tried
Robertson's remark that the list should shame all who are disposed to find fault with their lot, and his note that the word for robbers means brigands rather than thieves
themes: the care of all the churches

29.pericope_label: If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities
debates: What the burning means: Ellicott takes both words in their strongest sense, the stumbling of a grievous sin such as the temptations of the senses lead to, and a burning that elsewhere denotes sensual passion, so that men came with their tales of shame to a sympathy that entered even there; Robertson, Wesley and Barnes keep it to grief, and Clarke takes it of a burning zeal to restore the fallen

Whether the solemn appeal looks backward or forward: Barnes holds it made in view of the sufferings just recounted and not of what follows, since nothing in the escape at Damascus demanded so solemn an appeal, while Clarke and Calvin refer it forward to the incident that comes after, and Gill takes it of both together

How Damascus came to be under an Arabian king: Clarke explains it from the war that followed the divorce of that king’s daughter by Herod, and conjectures that the emperor’s death let him seize a favourable moment, while Robertson reports the absence of Roman coins in the city for a stretch of years and the suggestion that a later emperor gave it to him out of dislike for Herod

Why this particular escape closes the chapter: Ellicott finds in it an element of the ludicrous which gave occasion for jests, so that those who mocked his bodily presence would find matter for mirth, and Robertson calls it a humiliating experience in the city he had entered as a conqueror, while Calvin takes it as a first apprenticeship and finds its point in the closing of the gates of a royal city, which showed with what rage his enemies were inflamed
outliers: Clarke's attack on the reading of infirmities as indwelling sin, with his challenge that it would be difficult to produce a single passage in the whole New Testament where the word has the sense of sin or moral corruption

Barnes's note that philosophers, and the Stoics above all, counted every sympathetic feeling and all sensitiveness to suffering an infirmity, so that what the apostle gloried in they would have reckoned a weakness
Ellicott's grammatical note that the participle rendered which is is the form constantly used in the Greek Old Testament as the equivalent of the divine name, so that it renders He that is
Ellicott's conjecture that the solemn attestation was meant, as the words passed from his lips, to introduce a much fuller narrative than the one that actually followed
Clarke's distinction that nothing here countenances profane swearing, neither the exclamations of the surprised nor the appeals of men conscious of their own falsity who would gain credit by them

The difference of vocabulary between the two accounts of the escape, a rope-work hamper here against the general term in the history, which Robertson identifies as the basket of one of the miraculous feedings rather than the other
